items.question: What does MVCC let each SQL statement see, and why is this useful?
items.answer: Each statement sees a snapshot of a database version, protecting it from inconsistent data produced by concurrent updates.

evidence.quote: each SQL statement sees a snapshot of data

items.question: What is PostgreSQL's default transaction isolation level?
items.answer: Read Committed is the default isolation level.

evidence.quote: Read Committed is the default isolation level in PostgreSQL

items.question: Does PostgreSQL implement Read Uncommitted as a separate, weaker isolation mode?
items.answer: No. PostgreSQL implements three distinct isolation levels internally; Read Uncommitted behaves like Read Committed.

evidence.quote: PostgreSQL's Read Uncommitted mode behaves like Read Committed

items.question: If a transaction aborts after advancing a sequence, is that sequence change rolled back?
items.answer: No. Sequence changes are immediately visible to other transactions and are not rolled back when the transaction aborts.

evidence.quote: are immediately visible to all other transactions and are not rolled back

items.question: When does a Repeatable Read transaction fix its snapshot?
items.answer: At the start of its first non-transaction-control statement, rather than at the start of each subsequent statement.

evidence.quote: start of the first non-transaction-control statement in the transaction

items.question: What kind of lock can block an ordinary SELECT without FOR UPDATE or FOR SHARE?
items.answer: Only an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE table lock blocks an ordinary SELECT.

evidence.quote: Only an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock blocks a SELECT

items.question: Do row-level locks block ordinary reads, and when are they released?
items.answer: They block writers and lockers of the same row, not ordinary queries. They are released at transaction end or during savepoint rollback.

evidence.quote: Row-level locks do not affect data querying; they block only writers and lockers to the same row

items.question: Which system view shows outstanding database locks?
items.answer: The pg_locks system view.

evidence.quote: use the pg_locks system view

items.question: How does PostgreSQL resolve a detected deadlock? Can an application rely on which transaction is aborted?
items.answer: It aborts one of the involved transactions so the others can finish. Which transaction is aborted is not predictable and must not be relied upon.

evidence.quote: resolves them by aborting one of the transactions involved

items.question: Does a session-level advisory lock disappear if the transaction that acquired it rolls back?
items.answer: No. It remains held after rollback until explicitly released or the session ends.

evidence.quote: a lock acquired during a transaction that is later rolled back will still be held following the rollback

items.question: What SQLSTATE identifies a serialization failure?
items.answer: 40001, named serialization_failure.

evidence.quote: SQLSTATE code 40001 (serialization_failure)

items.question: What SQLSTATE identifies a detected deadlock?
items.answer: 40P01, named deadlock_detected.

evidence.quote: SQLSTATE code 40P01 (deadlock_detected)

items.question: On serialization failure, is retrying just the last SQL statement enough?
items.answer: No. Retry the complete transaction, including application logic deciding which SQL and values to use.

evidence.quote: retry the complete transaction, including all logic that decides which SQL to issue

items.question: Which DDL operations does this chapter identify as not MVCC-safe?
items.answer: TRUNCATE and table-rewriting forms of ALTER TABLE.

evidence.quote: TRUNCATE and the table-rewriting forms of ALTER TABLE, are not MVCC-safe

items.question: What is the strictest isolation level supported on a hot standby in this PostgreSQL 16 chapter?
items.answer: Repeatable Read; Serializable is not supported on hot standby replication targets.

evidence.quote: The strictest isolation level currently supported in hot standby mode is Repeatable Read

items.question: Which index type does the chapter recommend for concurrent applications indexing scalar data?
items.answer: B-tree indexes.

evidence.quote: B-tree indexes offer the best performance for concurrent applications

items.question: What lock mode represents Serializable predicate locks in pg_locks?
items.answer: SIReadLock.

evidence.quote: pg_locks system view with a mode of SIReadLock

items.question: Do PostgreSQL Serializable predicate locks cause blocking or deadlocks?
items.answer: The predicate locks themselves do not block and therefore cannot cause deadlocks; they track dependencies.

evidence.quote: these locks do not cause any blocking and therefore can not play any part in causing a deadlock

items.question: What happens to locks acquired after a savepoint when the transaction rolls back to that savepoint?
items.answer: They are released immediately.

evidence.quote: the lock is released immediately if the savepoint is rolled back to

items.question: How long are share/exclusive page-level locks on table pages normally held?
items.answer: They are released immediately after a row is fetched or updated.

evidence.quote: These locks are released immediately after a row is fetched or updated

items.question: Compare the snapshots used by Read Committed and Repeatable Read for two successive SELECT statements.
items.answer: Read Committed takes a new snapshot for each command and may see another transaction's intervening commit. Repeatable Read fixes the snapshot at its first non-transaction-control statement, so later SELECTs keep the same view.

evidence.quote: two successive SELECT commands can see different data
start of the first non-transaction-control statement in the transaction

items.question: Why can Repeatable Read still violate a business consistency rule, and what extra protection does Serializable add?
items.answer: A stable snapshot does not exclude serialization anomalies or cycles of read/write conflicts. Serializable monitors dangerous dependency patterns without additional ordinary blocking and rolls back a transaction to break a possible cycle.

evidence.quote: will not necessarily always be consistent with some serial
nonblocking monitoring for dangerous patterns of read/write conflicts

items.question: How do Read Committed and Repeatable Read handle a target row changed by a concurrent updater that then commits?
items.answer: Read Committed re-evaluates the WHERE condition on the updated row and may continue. Repeatable Read aborts with a serialization error if the row was actually changed after its snapshot; retry the whole transaction.

evidence.quote: The search condition of the command (the WHERE clause) is re-evaluated
the repeatable read transaction will be rolled back
retry the whole transaction from the beginning

items.question: Contrast the lifetime and rollback behavior of session-level and transaction-level advisory locks.
items.answer: Session locks survive transaction rollback until unlocked or the session ends; repeated acquisitions need matching unlocks. Transaction-level locks release automatically at transaction end with no explicit unlock. Advisory use is application-enforced.

evidence.quote: the system does not enforce their use
Transaction-level lock requests, on the other hand, behave more like regular lock requests

items.question: How should an application both reduce deadlock risk and recover from a deadlock that still happens?
items.answer: Acquire locks on objects in a consistent order, with the most restrictive needed mode first. If a transaction aborts due to a deadlock, it can be retried; deadlock_detected has SQLSTATE 40P01.

evidence.quote: acquire locks on multiple objects in a consistent order
SQLSTATE code 40P01 (deadlock_detected)

items.question: Is every unique-key violation safe to retry like SQLSTATE 40001? Explain the difference.
items.answer: Serialization failures 40001 should be retried. A 23505 unique violation or 23P01 exclusion violation can sometimes arise from concurrency, but can also be persistent; inspect the situation instead of blindly retrying all such failures.

evidence.quote: SQLSTATE code 40001 (serialization_failure)
they might represent persistent error conditions rather than transient failures

items.question: Why is an old Repeatable Read snapshot plus a newly acquired table lock insufficient for a current global consistency check?
items.answer: The snapshot may predate now-committed changes despite the lock. Under explicit locking, use Read Committed or acquire the required locks before Repeatable Read's first query freezes the snapshot; SHARE or stronger prevents other uncommitted changes in the locked table.

evidence.quote: A SHARE mode (or higher) lock guarantees that there are no uncommitted changes
be careful to obtain locks before performing queries
start of the first non-transaction-control statement in the transaction

items.question: Can an application assume that a Repeatable Read query on a hot standby has the same consistency guarantee as successful Serializable transactions on the primary?
items.answer: No. Serializable integrity protection does not extend to hot standby or logical replicas. Hot standby supports at most Repeatable Read and can temporarily show a state inconsistent with any serial execution of the primary transactions.

evidence.quote: does not yet extend to hot standby mode
can sometimes see a transient state that is inconsistent with any serial execution

items.question: Compare the lock granularity and release timing of B-tree and hash indexes, and explain the chapter's scalar-data recommendation.
items.answer: B-tree uses short-term page-level locks released after each index row. Hash uses bucket-level locks held until the bucket is processed, so deadlock is possible. The chapter recommends B-tree for concurrent scalar indexing.

evidence.quote: Locks are released immediately after each index row is fetched or inserted
Locks are released after the whole bucket is processed
recommended index type for concurrent applications that need to index scalar data

items.question: How is SERIALIZABLE READ ONLY DEFERRABLE different from an ordinary Serializable read, and why must ordinary transaction results wait for commit?
items.answer: A deferrable read-only transaction may wait for a safe snapshot, after which its reads are known valid. Other Serializable reads can belong to a transaction that later aborts, so their results must not be relied on before successful commit.

evidence.quote: not be considered valid until the transaction which read it has successfully committed
SERIALIZABLE READ ONLY DEFERRABLE transaction, it will block

items.question: Using Table 13.1, which anomalies are still possible under PostgreSQL Repeatable Read, and does it allow phantom reads?
items.answer: Serialization anomalies remain possible. Dirty, nonrepeatable and phantom reads are not possible in PostgreSQL Repeatable Read, which is stronger than the standard's minimum phantom-read guarantee.

evidence.quote: Repeatable read Not possible Not possible Allowed, but not in PG Possible
PostgreSQL's Repeatable Read implementation does not allow phantom reads

items.question: In Table 13.2, does a requested ROW EXCLUSIVE table lock conflict with an existing SHARE lock? What about an existing ACCESS SHARE lock?
items.answer: It conflicts with SHARE, but not ACCESS SHARE.

evidence.quote: Requested Lock Mode

items.question: According to Table 13.3, can FOR KEY SHARE coexist with FOR NO KEY UPDATE on the same row? Can it coexist with FOR UPDATE?
items.answer: It can coexist with FOR NO KEY UPDATE but conflicts with FOR UPDATE.

evidence.quote: Requested Lock Mode
SELECT FOR UPDATE is blocked, but not SELECT FOR NO KEY UPDATE

items.question: In the website.hits example starting with rows 9 and 10, why can DELETE WHERE hits = 10 delete nothing while a concurrent UPDATE increments both rows?
items.answer: The initial 9 row is not a target in the DELETE snapshot; the original 10 row is waited on and becomes 11 after UPDATE, so re-evaluating the condition fails. A row equal to 10 can exist before and after without being deleted.

evidence.quote: DELETE FROM website WHERE hits = 10
the new row value is no longer 10 but 11

items.question: In the mytab SUM example, can Serializable transactions A and B both commit after computing 30 and 300? Why would A-before-B require 330 instead?
items.answer: They cannot both commit; PostgreSQL aborts one to prevent a dependency anomaly. If A ran first, its inserted class-2 value 30 would be included in B's sum, making 330 rather than 300.

evidence.quote: will allow one transaction to commit and will roll the other back
if A had executed before B, B would have computed the sum 330, not 300

items.question: Why is SELECT pg_advisory_lock(id) FROM foo WHERE id > 12345 LIMIT 100 dangerous, and how does the chapter's subquery form avoid that hazard?
items.answer: LIMIT is not guaranteed to be applied before the locking function, so unexpected session locks can be acquired. Select the limited IDs in a subquery and apply pg_advisory_lock to its output, as in the documented safe form.

evidence.quote: SELECT pg_advisory_lock(q.id) FROM
the LIMIT is not guaranteed to be applied before the locking function is executed
